plants.summary: A planted hay legume, not a common wild plant, but ordinary on New England farms and in hay.
plants.identification: Three leaflets, the center one on a short stalk, and purple flower clusters. The seed pods spiral.
plants.lookalikes: Black medic is a low relative with yellow flowers and black pods. Clovers lack the stalked center leaflet.
plants.parts: Leaves and fine stems. Mature stems are woody.
plants.harvest: Cut at bud or early flower for the best feed. Lush wet alfalfa is a bloat risk for ruminants.
plants.preparation: Dried alfalfa hay is the usual form for rabbits. Wilt fresh cuttings before ruminants get them. Do not feed moldy hay.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: First cut is often late May or June in southern New England, later north. Later cuts follow through the summer if the stand is irrigated or the season is wet.

verdicts.label: Rabbit
verdicts.reason: House Rabbit Society treats alfalfa hay as suitable for growing rabbits and a limited hay for adults because of the calcium.
verdicts.notes: Fresh alfalfa is gassier than hay. Introduce it slowly.

verdicts.label: Chicken
verdicts.reason: Alfalfa is rich feed. Lush stands cause frothy bloat in cattle, sheep, and goats. Adult rabbits get more calcium than they need from a diet of alfalfa hay.
verdicts.notes: Dried hay is appropriate for growing rabbits. For adult rabbits, timothy or orchardgrass should be the usual hay. Ruminants should not get a sudden meal of wet alfalfa.

plants.summary: A clover with a poor reputation because of liver and photosensitivity disease, best documented in horses.
plants.identification: Upright, hairless, with a flower head that is white and pink on the same plant. Leaflets lack the white crescent of white clover.
plants.lookalikes: White clover creeps and the flower stalk is leafless. Red clover is hairy.
plants.parts: Not a chosen feed. If it is mixed into hay, it should not dominate the bale.
plants.harvest: Do not cut a pure stand to feed.
plants.preparation: Drying does not make a heavy alsike cutting a good feed.
plants.uncertainty: Disease reports are strongest for horses, which this guide does not cover. The limit for the other species is a caution, not a count of cases.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
Penn State Extension, forage and poisonous-plant publications.
plants.season_notes: Flowers in midsummer. It shows up in New England hay mixes and on damp ground.

verdicts.notes: A trace in mixed hay is a different situation from a bundle of alsike. Do not harvest it on purpose.

plants.summary: A common shrub. The leafy growth is not forage. Ripe fruit is a human food only after it is cooked, which is outside this guide.
plants.identification: A shrub with opposite compound leaves, white flat flower clusters, and dark berries. Twigs have a white pith.
plants.lookalikes: Pokeweed is an herb with alternate leaves and a red stem, and it is also toxic. Water hemlock is an herb, not a shrub, and is deadly.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves, bark, or unripe berries.
plants.harvest: Do not strip leafy stems for a basket.
plants.preparation: Do not dry the leaves for feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It flowers white in June and July in New England wet edges. Purple-black fruit follows. Leaves, stems, and unripe fruit are the cyanide problem.

citations.quote: Animals affected: Cattle, sheep Toxic principle: Cyanogenic glycoside sambunigrin which is hydrolysed in the rumen by microorganisms to free hydrogen cyanide (HCN). All parts of the plant are poisonous especially if wilted or in regrowth. The Cyanide blocks the action of cytochrome oxidase that prevents hemoglobin from releasing oxygen to the tissues.

plants.summary: A common New England yard and orchard tree. Fresh twigs are a rabbit chew. Wilted leaves are a cyanide risk.
plants.identification: Simple oval leaves with a fine tooth, and a fruit that is clearly an apple. Crabapples count as this entry.
plants.lookalikes: Cherry leaves are similar and smell like bitter almond when crushed. Cherry is a separate, stricter entry. If you are not sure it is apple, do not feed the leaves.
plants.parts: Fresh twigs in moderation. Not wilted leaves. Not seeds. Fruit flesh only as a small treat.
plants.harvest: Offer prunings fresh, the same day, or not at all. Do not feed a pile of leaves that sat and wilted.
plants.preparation: Do not dry apple leaves for feed. Remove seeds if you offer fruit. A whole apple is a lot of sugar for a rabbit.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: Twigs can be cut in winter and early spring. Leaves are on the tree from May to October. Wilted leaves after a storm or a pruning pile are the dangerous form. Fruit drops in September and October.

verdicts.label: Rabbit
verdicts.reason: Apple leaves and seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides. Wilted leaves are the dangerous form, the same class of problem as cherry. Fresh twigs are a common rabbit chew and are a lower risk than a pile of wilted leaves.
verdicts.notes: Feed fresh twigs. Do not feed wilted leaves or seeds.
verdicts.amount: About 1 teaspoon per 2 lb of body weight a day. Fruit stays under 10% of the diet. No stem or seeds.

plants.summary: A yellow-flowered pasture legume that is less likely to cause bloat than alfalfa or clover.
plants.identification: Five leaflets (three at the tip, two at the base) and yellow pea flowers. The pods spread like a bird's foot.
plants.lookalikes: Crown vetch has pink flowers and climbs. Yellow sweet clover is much taller, with tiny flowers along the stem.
plants.parts: Leafy tops.
plants.harvest: Cut in flower or just before. It is a pasture plant more than a bulk hay plant.
plants.preparation: Fresh or dried, as part of a mix. It contains tannins, which is why bloat is less common, and those tannins are a reason not to overdo it.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
Penn State Extension, forage and poisonous-plant publications.
Langston University, E (Kika) de la Garza American Institute for Goat Research, goat nutrition materials.
plants.season_notes: Flowers and pods in July and August. It is planted in New England pastures and also escapes.

plants.summary: A climbing nightshade. It is not oriental bittersweet, which is a woody vine with red and yellow capsules.
plants.identification: Purple flowers with yellow centers and bright red egg-shaped berries. Leaves are often lobed at the base.
plants.lookalikes: Oriental bittersweet is a woody twiner with orange capsules that split to show red seeds. That vine is not this plant, and it is not a feed either.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves or berries.
plants.harvest: Do not strip it off a fence for animals.
plants.preparation: Cooking is not a step in this guide. Leave the plant.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It vines through New England hedges and flowers and fruits from midsummer into fall.

plants.summary: A common New England tree. Wilted leaves release cyanide.
plants.identification: Alternate simple leaves, fine teeth, and a scratch on the twig that smells like bitter almond. Mature bark looks like burnt cornflakes. White flower spikes, then dark fruit.
plants.lookalikes: Apple leaves do not smell of bitter almond. If a crushed leaf or scratched twig smells like almond, treat it as cherry and do not feed it.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves or wilted twigs. Fruit is not the forage product.
plants.harvest: Do not throw prunings over the fence.
plants.preparation: Wilting increases the danger. Do not dry the leaves for feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: Leaves are dangerous whenever they wilt, which in New England includes summer storm damage and the fall of leaves. Pin cherry and chokecherry deserve the same refusal.

plants.summary: A planted and escaped tree. It is poisonous. Honey locust, which has large branched thorns and long pods, is a different tree and is still not a recommended feed here.
plants.identification: Compound leaves, a pair of short thorns at the nodes, and hanging clusters of white pea flowers. The pods are flat.
plants.lookalikes: Honey locust has much larger branched thorns and long twisted pods. Do not feed either on the strength of the other.
plants.parts: Do not feed bark, seeds, leaves, or sprouts.
plants.harvest: Do not toss locust prunings into a pen.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes it feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It flowers white in late May and June along New England fences and roads. Bark, sprouts, and seeds are the worst parts.

plants.summary: A bramble. Leaves are a standard rabbit green and goat browse. Other Rubus species in the region, including black raspberry, are used the same way.
plants.identification: Arching canes with thorns, leaves usually in fives, and white flowers followed by black aggregate fruit that does not slip off a core.
plants.lookalikes: Multiflora rose has a different flower and a hip, not a blackberry. Poison ivy can thread through a bramble patch and has three glossy leaflets and no thorns.
plants.parts: Leaves and young cane tips. Fruit is fine for poultry and pigs in season. Thorns are the practical limit for the person cutting it and for wool.
plants.harvest: Clip leafy tips with gloves. Leave the old woody cane.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh or dry the leaves. No wilting is required for safety.
sources: House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
Langston University, E (Kika) de la Garza American Institute for Goat Research, goat nutrition materials.
ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.
plants.season_notes: Leaves are useful from May until frost. Fruit ripens in late July and August in much of New England, later in the north.

plants.summary: A native fern that causes a serious poisoning, including bone-marrow failure and tumors in cattle, and thiamine deficiency in horses.
plants.identification: A single coarse triangular frond, divided, often waist-high, rising separately from a underground rhizome rather than in a crown.
plants.lookalikes: Ostrich fern grows in a crown in floodplains and is not a livestock feed either. If you cannot name the fern, do not feed it. This guide does not treat other ferns as forage.
plants.parts: Do not feed fronds, fresh or dried.
plants.harvest: Keep bracken out of hay cuttings.
plants.preparation: Drying does not remove the toxin. There is no safe amount to aim for.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: Fiddleheads appear in May. Fronds are toxic through the summer and in dried hay. It is common on New England dry slopes and old fields.

plants.summary: A common meadow flower. Fresh plants blister mouths.
plants.identification: Shiny yellow flowers with five petals and divided leaves. Several species grow in New England. All fresh buttercups get the same caution.
plants.lookalikes: Cinquefoil has strawberry-like leaves and is not this plant. Lesser celandine grows low and wet in early spring and is also not a feed.
plants.parts: Do not feed fresh plants.
plants.harvest: Do not add buttercup to a fresh bundle.
plants.preparation: This guide is about fresh harvest. Do not cut buttercup for fresh feed. Hay that is fully dry is a different product, and a bale that is mostly buttercup is still poor feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: Flowers from May into July in New England hay meadows. The fresh plant is the problem. Fully dried hay loses most of the irritant.

plants.summary: The tops of the carrot you planted. They are a normal rabbit green. They are not Queen Anne's lace from the roadside.
plants.identification: Feathery leaves from a known garden row or from carrots you bought.
plants.lookalikes: Poison hemlock leaves are finer and the plant is hairless with a spotted stem. Do not go to a roadside to cut carrot tops.
plants.parts: Leaves of garden carrots. Roots are a treat, not forage.
plants.harvest: Cut tops from your row or use tops from carrots you bought. Wash them.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh. A large amount from heavily fertilized ground is unnecessary because of nitrate.
sources: House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.
plants.season_notes: Garden carrot tops are available from July until the roots are dug, often into October.

plants.summary: A garden herb with a long reputation as feed and a real pyrrolizidine-alkaloid problem. It is not a forage.
plants.identification: Large hairy leaves, the upper ones running down the stem, and clusters of nodding pink, purple, or white bells.
plants.lookalikes: Foxglove has smoother leaves and thimble flowers on a tall spike, and is also toxic. Do not guess between them.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves.
plants.harvest: Do not cut it for animals.
plants.preparation: Drying does not remove pyrrolizidine alkaloids.
sources: Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
plants.season_notes: Garden plants leaf out in May and flower through the summer. It is planted in New England gardens and persists for years.

plants.summary: A cool-season garden weed used as a small green for rabbits and poultry.
plants.identification: A low mat, opposite leaves, and a line of hairs on one side of the stem. Small white flowers with five petals so deeply split they look like ten.
plants.lookalikes: Scarlet pimpernel, which is not a feed here, has orange or blue flowers and no hair line on the stem. Mouse-ear chickweed is hairier.
plants.parts: Tender tops.
plants.harvest: Cut the tops. Do not take a mat full of soil.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh, in a mix. Very large amounts are unnecessary. It wilts fast, which is fine.
sources: House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.
University of Maine Cooperative Extension, forage guidance.
plants.season_notes: Best in April, May, and again in September and October. It can linger in a mild early winter in southern New England. Summer plants are stringy.

plants.summary: A native milkweed. The latex is poisonous. It is not forage, even though insects eat it.
plants.identification: Opposite, thick, oval leaves, a stout stem, milky sap, and round clusters of dusty-pink flowers. Pods are warty.
plants.lookalikes: Dogbane also has milky sap and is poisonous. Spreading dogbane is branched with smaller pods. Either plant stays out of the basket.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves, pods, or flowers.
plants.harvest: Do not cut it for feed.
plants.preparation: Drying does not make milkweed a safe green.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It is in full leaf from June through August along New England fields and roads.

plants.summary: A roadside weed that causes sunburn in light-skinned stock.
plants.identification: Yellow flowers with five petals and many stamens. Hold a leaf to the light: it looks perforated with tiny clear dots.
plants.lookalikes: Other yellow weeds lack those translucent dots. If you do not see them, you are not looking at this plant, and an unnamed yellow weed is still not automatically safe.
plants.parts: Do not feed tops or hay made from a heavy stand.
plants.harvest: Leave it out of the cutting.
plants.preparation: Drying does not remove hypericin.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It flowers along New England roads in July. The photosensitizing pigment is in the fresh plant and in hay.

verdicts.label: Rabbit
verdicts.reason: Hypericin in St. John's wort causes photosensitization: unpigmented skin blisters in the sun. Cattle, sheep, and goats are the usual cases.
verdicts.notes: Do not feed it, and do not turn light-skinned animals onto a stand of it.

plants.summary: A weedy grass that livestock and poultry take readily.
plants.identification: Stems that root at the nodes and spread like a crab. Finger-like seed heads.
plants.lookalikes: Foxtail has a bristly cylindrical head. Those bristles can injure mouths, so do not substitute foxtail for this plant.
plants.parts: Leaves and tender stems. Skip bristly seed heads of any grass mixed in.
plants.harvest: Pull or cut the leafy growth. Shake out soil.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh the same day. Piles of crabgrass heat quickly.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.
University of Maine Cooperative Extension, forage guidance.
plants.season_notes: A summer annual. In New England it is useful from July until frost, especially in gardens and beaten ground.

plants.summary: A pink-flowered roadside legume that is poisonous, not a forage vetch.
plants.identification: Sprawling stems, compound leaves, and a circle of pink-and-white pea flowers. Seed pods are slender.
plants.lookalikes: Birdsfoot trefoil has yellow flowers. Hairy vetch has purple flowers and obviously hairy stems.
plants.parts: Do not feed any part.
plants.harvest: Keep it out of the basket.
plants.preparation: There is no preparation that makes it a feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It flowers along New England roads from June into August. It was planted for erosion control and escaped.

plants.summary: A common New England weed. Oxalate is the reason to limit it. Sheep sorrel is a smaller relative with the same caution.
plants.identification: Long leaves with wavy margins in a rosette, and a tall stalk of green flowers that turns rusty brown.
plants.lookalikes: Burdock has huge heart-shaped leaves that are not wavy in the same way. Skunk cabbage grows in wet muck and smells skunky when torn.
plants.parts: Young leaves, sparingly. Not the seed stalk.
plants.harvest: Take a few leaves from a plant, not the whole stand.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh and limited. Drying does not remove oxalate.
sources: Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
Penn State Extension, forage and poisonous-plant publications.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: Basal leaves are best in May and June. The rusty seed stalks stand through fall and are not the feed.

plants.summary: A spring bulb. Alkaloids make the bulbs and leaves poisonous.
plants.identification: Strap leaves and a yellow or white flower with a trumpet, from a bulb.
plants.lookalikes: Iris has a flat fan of leaves and a different flower, and it is not given a safe verdict here either. If it is a spring bulb, do not feed it.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves or bulbs.
plants.harvest: Do not toss divided bulbs to pigs or poultry.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes it feed.
sources: Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center toxic-plant list, used here as a companion-animal caution alongside a veterinary source.
Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
plants.season_notes: Leaves come up in April and May across New England yards. Bulbs are in the ground all year and are the most dangerous part.

plants.summary: A common New England green for rabbits and poultry, and a normal part of pasture.
plants.identification: A basal rosette of toothed leaves, hollow flower stalks, and a single yellow head. The plant has milky sap.
plants.lookalikes: Catsear has branched, solid stalks and hairy leaves. Hawkweeds are hairy. Those are not substitutes without their own identification.
plants.parts: Leaves and flowers. Roots are not needed for feed.
plants.harvest: Cut leaves from unsprayed ground. Wash grit off. Skip plants from a chemically treated lawn.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh or dry the leaves. No wilting is required for safety. Large wet amounts can loosen stools.
sources: House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.
University of Maine Cooperative Extension, forage guidance.
plants.season_notes: The best leaves are April through early June, then again in September and October. Midsummer leaves are bitter. Flowers follow the spring leaves.

plants.summary: A tall native of wet ground. Steroidal alkaloids cause severe poisoning and birth defects.
plants.identification: Broad, pleated leaves that clasp a stout stem, in wet soil. The flower cluster is a branching green-yellow spike.
plants.lookalikes: Skunk cabbage has leaves that come from the ground, not up a tall stem, and it smells skunky. Both are toxic. Indian poke is another name for false hellebore, not for a table vegetable.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves or roots.
plants.harvest: Do not cut it.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes it feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It stands in wet New England meadows and streambanks from May into July. All of the above-ground growth is dangerous.

plants.summary: An invasive mustard. It is not a studied livestock feed, and it smells of garlic.
plants.identification: Heart-shaped toothed leaves, a garlic smell when crushed, and small white flowers with four petals in the second year.
plants.lookalikes: Violets do not smell of garlic. Ground ivy creeps and has scalloped round leaves.
plants.parts: Not a recommended feed. Pulling it for disposal is a different job from feeding it.
plants.harvest: Do not add it to a forage basket.
plants.preparation: There is no preparation step that turns it into a recommended feed.
plants.uncertainty: Livestock feeding trials are thin. The limit is a caution based on its chemistry, not a list of poisoning cases.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: Rosettes overwinter. The best leaves are April and May, before the white flowers set seed. It is a serious New England woodland invasive.

plants.summary: An invasive shrub with a laxative toxin in the bark and fruit.
plants.identification: Alternate glossy leaves with smooth edges, small pale flowers, and berries that turn from red to black. The bark, scraped, is yellow-orange inside. Common buckthorn has toothed leaves and often a thorn at the tip.
plants.lookalikes: Alder grows in the same wet places and is not a feed in this guide. Cherry smells like bitter almond. If you are looking at buckthorn, do not feed it.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves, bark, or berries.
plants.harvest: Do not cut it for animals.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes it feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It leafs out early and keeps leaves late. It is an invasive shrub of New England wetlands and old fields. Common buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica) gets the same verdict.

plants.summary: A creeping mint, also called creeping Charlie. It is treated as poisonous to horses and is not a feed here.
plants.identification: Scalloped round leaves on a creeping square stem, and purple flowers in the leaf axils. It smells minty when crushed.
plants.lookalikes: Violets have heart-shaped leaves and do not creep the same way. Garlic mustard smells of garlic and does not creep into a mat.
plants.parts: Do not feed it.
plants.harvest: Do not add lawn mats of ground ivy to clippings.
plants.preparation: Drying is not a reason to feed it.
plants.uncertainty: The strongest reports are in horses. It is still marked toxic here rather than offered as a feed.

plants.season_notes: It is green in April and May and again in the cool fall, often under shrubs and in lawns.

plants.summary: A native shrub. The fruit is the part animals actually get. Leaves are not a bulk feed.
plants.identification: An upright shrub, alternate oval leaves, white urn-shaped flowers, and blue berries with a bloom.
plants.lookalikes: Sheep laurel has pink saucer flowers and opposite or whorled leaves and is deadly. If the shrub is evergreen with pink saucers, it is not blueberry.
plants.parts: Ripe berries as a treat. Leaves only in a small accidental amount.
plants.harvest: Pick berries. Do not cut the bushes for leaf fodder.
plants.preparation: Feed fruit fresh, in modest amounts. It is sugar, not a forage base.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.
University of Maine Cooperative Extension, forage guidance.
plants.season_notes: Fruit ripens in July and August in most of New England, earlier on warm coastal sites, later in the mountains and in Maine.

plants.summary: A spiny pasture nightshade. Animals usually avoid it, and it is still a poisoning plant when they do not.
plants.identification: Spiny stems and leaves, potato-like purple or white flowers, and yellow berries.
plants.lookalikes: Potato flowers look similar. Potato vines are toxic too. A spiny plant in the pasture with potato flowers is horsenettle.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves or berries.
plants.harvest: Do not include it in a cutting.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes it feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
Penn State Extension, forage and poisonous-plant publications.
plants.season_notes: It stands in New England pastures from June until frost, with yellow berries late in the season.

plants.summary: A woodland arum. Calcium oxalate crystals burn the mouth.
plants.identification: One or two leaves, each with three leaflets, and a hooded flower (the spathe) around a club (the spadix).
plants.lookalikes: Trillium also has parts in threes but the flower is not a hooded jack. If you are looking at a hooded flower in the woods, do not feed it.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves, corm, or berries.
plants.harvest: Do not dig or cut it for animals.
plants.preparation: Drying does not make the crystals a reason to experiment.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It is up in New England woods in May and June. The red fruit cluster comes later and is not feed.

plants.summary: A tropane-alkaloid plant. Seeds and leaves are both dangerous.
plants.identification: Large toothed leaves, a foul smell, white or pale purple trumpet flowers, and a spiny egg-shaped pod.
plants.lookalikes: Ground cherry has a papery husk and is not a reason to experiment. If the plant has a spiny pod and a trumpet flower, do not feed it.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves, flowers, or seeds.
plants.harvest: Pull it away from pens. Do not put it in the feed.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes it feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It appears in New England barnyards and gardens in midsummer and carries spiny pods into frost.

plants.summary: A cold-hardy garden brassica. Gas and goitrogens are the limit, and kale anemia is a cattle problem when the intake is high.
plants.identification: Blue-green curly or flat leaves on a plant you planted. Broccoli and cabbage leaves count as this entry.
plants.lookalikes: Comfrey is hairy with bell flowers and is toxic. Do not grab a large garden leaf without knowing it.
plants.parts: Leaves, in moderation.
plants.harvest: Cut leaves, not a wheelbarrow of them for a few rabbits.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh and limited. Do not feed a sudden large amount to cattle or sheep.
sources: House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.
plants.season_notes: Spring plantings are cut from June. Fall plantings hold into November and, in southern New England, through many winters. Cabbage, collards, and broccoli leaves are the same species and the same limit.

verdicts.label: Rabbit
verdicts.reason: House Rabbit Society lists kale (all types) among the leafy greens that are safe for rabbits. Introduce it slowly, like any new green.
verdicts.notes: A leaf or two for a rabbit, or a small share of a mix, is the usual limit. Do not switch cattle onto a field of kale all at once.
verdicts.amount: Leafy greens make up about 75% of the fresh portion of the diet.

plants.summary: A common lawn and pasture grass across New England.
plants.identification: A boat-shaped leaf tip and a fine, dark green sod. The flower head is an open pyramid.
plants.lookalikes: Annual bluegrass is paler and seeds low to the ground. Quackgrass has clasping auricles at the leaf base.
plants.parts: Leaves. Skip seed heads once they are dry and stemmy.
plants.harvest: Only cut plants you know have not been treated with lawn herbicide or insecticide.
plants.preparation: Feed small amounts fresh, or dry them. Lawn clippings heat and mold quickly, so feed them the same day or not at all.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
University of Maine Cooperative Extension, forage guidance.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: It greens up in April and May and grows again in the cool fall. It stalls in hot, dry July weather.

plants.summary: A common garden weed. Poultry and pigs eat it. Nitrate and oxalate set the limit.
plants.identification: Diamond-shaped leaves with a white mealy coating, especially on the growing tips.
plants.lookalikes: Pigweed (Amaranthus) has a coarser stem and no white meal on the tip. Nightshades have different flowers and berries and are toxic.
plants.parts: Young tops only, and not from heavily fertilized ground.
plants.harvest: Cut young plants. Skip thick stands on old manure piles.
plants.preparation: Feed a limited fresh amount. Do not ferment a large mass of it.
sources: ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
Penn State Extension, forage and poisonous-plant publications.
plants.season_notes: From June until it goes to seed in late summer. Plants on rich garden soil can accumulate nitrate.

plants.summary: A garden green. Leaf and romaine types are the useful ones. Iceberg is mostly water.
plants.identification: The plant you sowed: a head or loose leaves, milky sap when the stem is cut, and no strong odor.
plants.lookalikes: Wild lettuce is a different, more bitter plant and is not given the same verdict here. Feed the garden plant you know.
plants.parts: Leaves. Not a diet of it.
plants.harvest: Cut outer leaves or a whole head you grew or bought. Wash it.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh. Do not feed spoiled, slimy leaves. Iceberg is poor nutrition and is the one to skip.
sources: House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.
plants.season_notes: Garden lettuce is cut from May until a hard frost if it is replanted. It bolts and turns bitter in July heat.

verdicts.label: Rabbit
verdicts.reason: Leaf lettuce and romaine are standard rabbit and poultry greens. They are mostly water, so they supplement a real diet.
verdicts.notes: Skip iceberg. Do not feed a rabbit a meal of only lettuce.
verdicts.amount: Leafy greens make up about 75% of the fresh portion of the diet.

plants.summary: A garden groundcover with cardiac glycosides.
plants.identification: Two broad basal leaves and a one-sided stalk of small white bells, then red berries.
plants.lookalikes: Wild lily of the valley (Maianthemum) is a smaller woodland plant and is not a feed either. Ramps smell strongly of onion and are an Allium, which is its own toxic entry.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves, flowers, berries, or roots.
plants.harvest: Do not pull the patch for animals.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes it feed.
sources: Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center toxic-plant list, used here as a companion-animal caution alongside a veterinary source.
plants.season_notes: It flowers in May in New England shade gardens and persists as a groundcover. Leaves and rhizomes are present through the summer.

plants.summary: An evergreen shrub with the same class of toxin as sheep laurel and rhododendron.
plants.identification: A taller evergreen shrub, glossy alternate leaves, and terminal clusters of pink or white saucer flowers with ten pockets.
plants.lookalikes: Rhododendron and azalea are in the same toxic group. Sheep laurel is lower and flowers along the stem. Do not feed any of them.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves or clippings.
plants.harvest: Do not dump prunings where stock can reach them.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes it feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It flowers in June. It is common in Connecticut, Rhode Island, and Massachusetts and present in southern parts of the northern states. Leaves are toxic whenever they are green.

plants.summary: An invasive rose. Goats are often used to knock it back. The leaves are browse, not a poisonous plant.
plants.identification: Arching canes, fringed stipules at the leaf base, clusters of small white flowers, then small red hips. Thorns are recurved.
plants.lookalikes: Blackberry has aggregate fruit, not a hip. Native roses are not a reason to skip identification, but the feeding note is similar if you are sure it is a rose and not a bramble mixed with poison ivy.
plants.parts: Leaves and young tips. Hips are not the main feed.
plants.harvest: Cut tips with heavy gloves. It will take over a field if you only cut a little and leave the crowns.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh. Thorns are the limit, especially for sheep because of the wool.
sources: Langston University, E (Kika) de la Garza American Institute for Goat Research, goat nutrition materials.
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
University of Maine Cooperative Extension, forage guidance.
plants.season_notes: Leaves from May until frost. White flower clusters in June. It is a widespread New England invasive.

plants.summary: An Allium. It causes red-blood-cell damage. It does not belong in a forage basket.
plants.identification: Hollow or flat blue-green leaves in a bulb you planted, with the familiar onion smell.
plants.lookalikes: Garlic mustard smells of garlic but is a broad-leaved invasive. Both stay out of the feed.
plants.parts: Do not feed bulbs, leaves, or trimmings.
plants.harvest: Do not dump kitchen onion scraps into the poultry pen or the rabbit greens.
plants.preparation: Cooking is not a step that makes a pile of onions into forage.
sources: Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: Garden onions are pulled in late summer. Chives, garlic, and leeks are the same refusal all season.

verdicts.label: Rabbit

verdicts.notes: Do not feed kitchen scraps of onion or garlic.

plants.summary: A common New England pasture and hay grass, especially where snow cover is reliable.
plants.identification: Clumped plant with a flattened stem base. The flower head is branched, with clumps of spikelets, not a single tight cylinder.
plants.lookalikes: Timothy has one dense cylindrical head. Tall fescue has a coarser leaf and often reddish stem bases.
plants.parts: Leaves and stems.
plants.harvest: Cut leaf growth and leave the crown. Older stems are poor feed.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh or as hay. Discard moldy material.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.

House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: Leaves are usable from May into October. The bunched seed heads show in late May and June. Later growth stays leafy if it is cut before it gets coarse.

plants.summary: A lawn and path weed fed as a minor green.
plants.identification: Broad oval leaves with parallel veins, in a rosette. The flower is a green spike. English plantain has lance leaves and a similar spike.
plants.lookalikes: Some lilies send up strap leaves, but they lack the parallel-veined rosette and the green spike. If the plant is not clearly plantain, leave it.
plants.parts: Leaves of both common and English plantain.
plants.harvest: Cut leaves, not the tough flower spikes. Avoid sprayed lawns.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh or dried. No special wilting.
sources: House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.

plants.summary: One of the deadly parsleys. A small amount can kill. All parts are poisonous.
plants.identification: A hairless stem with purple spots, finely divided parsley-like leaves, a musty smell, and white umbrella-shaped flower clusters.
plants.lookalikes: Queen Anne's lace has a hairy stem and smells like carrot. Water hemlock grows in wetter ground and has chambered roots. If you are not sure, do not cut any of them.
plants.parts: Do not feed any part, including the root.
plants.harvest: Do not put it in a basket. Do not compost it into a pen.
plants.preparation: There is no drying or cooking step in this guide that makes it feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: Rosettes are green in spring. Tall spotted stems and white flowers appear in June and July along New England roads, ditches, and waste ground.

plants.summary: Not a cut-and-carry plant. The person cutting it is the one who gets hurt. Goats often eat it and are a special case below.
plants.identification: Three leaflets, the center one on a longer stalk, often shiny, and a woody vine or low shrub. White berries late in the year. No thorns.
plants.lookalikes: Virginia creeper usually has five leaflets. Blackberry has thorns and five leaflets. Raspberry has thorns. When in doubt, do not touch it.
plants.parts: Do not cut it by hand for any animal.
plants.harvest: Do not put it in a basket, a wheelbarrow of greens, or a hay pile.
plants.preparation: There is no safe handling method offered here.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Langston University, E (Kika) de la Garza American Institute for Goat Research, goat nutrition materials.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It leafs out in May and is a handling hazard until the leaves are gone. Vines and low plants are both common across New England.

disputes.topic: Verdict for Rabbit, Chicken, Duck, Goose, Turkey, Quail, Guinea pig, Goat, Sheep, Pig, Cattle
disputes.note: Colorado State University and the University of Arkansas Extension say animals are unaffected by poison ivy. We keep it cautious because the oil on coats and in manure harms the people who handle them, and we found no source that confirms it is safe feed for every animal listed here.

citations.title: Poison ivy (Toxicodendron radicans (L.) Kuntze)
citations.publisher: Colorado State University College of Veterinary Medicine, Guide to Poisonous Plants
citations.quote: Animals affected: Animals are not affected by poison ivy. People are primarily sensitive to the irritant oil in the plant. Toxic principle: The leaves and stems contain an irritant oil called urushiol that is released from the crushed or broken surface of the leaves or stems. Special notes: Poison ivy is usually not a problem to animals. However, the irritant oil can be present on the hair of animals that have contacted poison ivy, and can therefore be a problem to people handling the animal. Handling of the feces of cattle, sheep or goats that eat poison ivy can also cause an allergic response.

citations.quote: Poison Ivy (Toxicodendron radicans) • Toxic Principle: phenolic compound urushiol • Mucous and membrane irritant • No effect on livestock. • Breathing smoke may cause irritation.

plants.summary: A tall native plant of New England edges and gardens. It is poisonous. The berries stain and tempt people who have heard they are food.
plants.identification: Large alternate leaves, a red-purple stem, and drooping clusters of dark purple berries. The plant can be taller than a person.
plants.lookalikes: Elderberry is a woody shrub with opposite leaves and red-purple stems on a bush, not this herb. Neither is a safe leafy feed.
plants.parts: Do not feed shoots, leaves, berries, or roots.
plants.harvest: Do not cut it for a basket.
plants.preparation: No livestock preparation makes pokeweed feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: Shoots come up in May. Berries ripen purple in late summer and fall. The root is the most toxic part and is present all season.

plants.summary: The vine and any green tuber are poisonous. This is not a feed entry for cooked kitchen potatoes.
plants.identification: Compound leaves on a plant you planted, white or purple flowers, and tubers underground.
plants.lookalikes: Tomato vines are hairier and smell stronger. Horsenettle is spiny. All three are toxic.
plants.parts: Do not feed vines, green tubers, or sprouted green skin.
plants.harvest: Do not throw the pulled vines to livestock.
plants.preparation: No preparation in this guide turns the vine into feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: Vines are green from June until they die back. Green tubers show up at harvest, late summer and fall.

plants.summary: A succulent garden weed. Poultry take it readily. Oxalate is the limit.
plants.identification: Thick red stems, fleshy oval leaves, and small yellow flowers. The plant sprawls.
plants.lookalikes: Spurge has milky sap and is not purslane. If the broken stem bleeds white latex, do not feed it.
plants.parts: Stems and leaves, in moderation.
plants.harvest: Cut above the soil. Confirm there is no milky sap.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh. Do not make it the whole basket, because of oxalate.
sources: ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: A heat weed. In New England it is worth cutting from July until frost, mostly in gardens and bare soil.

plants.summary: A poplar used as browse. Bigtooth aspen is similar. Bark in large amounts is the part to avoid.
plants.identification: Rounded leaves that tremble, flattened leaf stalks, and smooth pale bark on young trees.
plants.lookalikes: Birch has a different bark and toothed leaves that do not tremble on flat stalks. Cherry smells like bitter almond when a twig is scratched.
plants.parts: Leaves and small twigs. Not slabs of bark.
plants.harvest: Cut small branches. Do not strip a trunk.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh. A normal browse portion, not a diet of bark.
sources: Langston University, E (Kika) de la Garza American Institute for Goat Research, goat nutrition materials.
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: Twigs and young leaves from late spring through summer. Winter twigs are browse when the leaves are gone. It is common in northern New England.

plants.summary: Wild carrot. The plant itself is a minor green. The emergency is mistaking poison hemlock or water hemlock for it.
plants.identification: A hairy stem, a carrot smell, white flat flower clusters often with one dark floret in the center, and a nest-like seed head that curls inward.
plants.lookalikes: Poison hemlock is hairless, with purple spots on the stem and a musty smell. Water hemlock grows in wet ground, is hairless, and has chambered roots. If the stem is smooth, do not call it Queen Anne's lace.
plants.parts: Only a correctly identified plant, and only a small amount of leaf. When there is any doubt, feed none of it.
plants.harvest: If you cannot separate it from hemlock with certainty, do not cut umbels at all.
plants.preparation: There is no preparation that fixes a wrong identification.
plants.uncertainty: Do not harvest white umbels unless the hairy stem and carrot smell are obvious.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: White flowers in July and August. The first-year rosette is around earlier. The identification risk is highest when only leaves are present.

verdicts.label: Rabbit
verdicts.reason: A correctly identified wild carrot is a carrot relative, not a hemlock. The limit stands because a mistake is fatal and because some umbels are phototoxic.
verdicts.notes: If the stem is hairless or purple-spotted, or the plant is in standing water, stop. That is not this entry.

plants.summary: A hay and pasture clover, upright, with pink-purple heads.
plants.identification: Three leaflets with a pale mark, hairy stems, and a pink head sitting close to the upper leaves.
plants.lookalikes: Alsike clover is finer, not hairy, with a pink-and-white head. White clover creeps.
plants.parts: Leaves and young flower heads, sparingly.
plants.harvest: Skip plants with lots of brown leaf blotches. Do not make it the whole cutting.
plants.preparation: Wilt before feeding ruminants. Dry hay is safer than lush wet clover. Discard mold.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
Penn State Extension, forage and poisonous-plant publications.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: Cut leaf and early flower from June into August. Plants with brown patches on the leaves may carry the fungus associated with slobbers.

verdicts.label: Rabbit
verdicts.reason: Red clover shares the bloat risk of other clovers. It also contains phytoestrogens. A leaf fungus (black patch) is tied to slobbers, which is saliva and irritation best known in horses.
verdicts.notes: Use a small share of a mix. Do not feed blotched, moldy clover.

plants.summary: A common swamp and yard maple. Wilted leaves cause red-blood-cell destruction, best documented in horses.
plants.identification: Opposite leaves with sharper teeth than a sugar maple, red buds and often red leaf stalks, and red fall color. It tolerates wet ground.
plants.lookalikes: Sugar maple has smoother lobes and brown buds. If you cannot tell them apart, feed neither. Oak leaves are alternate, not opposite.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves. Do not feed wilted branch prunings.
plants.harvest: Do not toss storm-downed maple limbs into a pen.
plants.preparation: Drying and wilting are the problem, not the cure.
plants.uncertainty: Case reports are concentrated in horses. Other species are marked toxic as a precaution, not because each has a large case series.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: The dangerous New England window is wilted or fallen leaves, especially after a storm and in September and October. Spring leaves are not a feed either.

plants.summary: Garden and wild red raspberry. Leaves are used like blackberry leaves.
plants.identification: Upright canes with a whitish bloom, leaves usually in threes, and a red fruit that slips off the core.
plants.lookalikes: Blackberry fruit keeps its core. Wineberry, an invasive, has red hairs on the cane. Wineberry leaves are not a separate entry; do not assume every cane is raspberry.
plants.parts: Leaves and tender tips. Ripe fruit as a small treat for poultry and pigs.
plants.harvest: Cut leafy tips, not the whole cane.
plants.preparation: Fresh or dried leaves. No special wilting.
sources: House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.
Langston University, E (Kika) de la Garza American Institute for Goat Research, goat nutrition materials.
plants.season_notes: Leaves from May through August. Fruit in July in southern New England, later north.

verdicts.notes: Keep the portion modest. Thorns are a handling problem, not a toxin.
verdicts.amount: Leafy greens make up about 75% of the fresh portion of the diet.

plants.summary: A coarse garden and barnyard weed. Nitrate is the hazard.
plants.identification: A red taproot, oval leaves, and a bristly green flower cluster. The stem is rough.
plants.lookalikes: Lambsquarters has a white mealy tip. Spiny amaranth has sharp spines and should be left alone.
plants.parts: Young leaves, if at all, and never a cartload from rich ground.
plants.harvest: Skip plants that were drought-stressed and then heavily manured.
plants.preparation: There is no home preparation that removes nitrate.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
Penn State Extension, forage and poisonous-plant publications.
plants.season_notes: Midsummer into early fall. Nitrate is highest in stressed or heavily fertilized plants, which are common in gardens and barnyards.

verdicts.label: Rabbit

verdicts.notes: A few young leaves in a mix are a different risk from a trough of pigweed. When in doubt, leave the stand.

plants.summary: A tall wetland grass along New England ditches, streams, and wet meadows.
plants.identification: Broad leaves and a straw-colored, open seed head. It forms dense stands in wet soil. Ligule is prominent.
plants.lookalikes: Orchardgrass is an upland clump grass. Reed canarygrass is wetter and taller.
plants.parts: Young leaves only, and only in a mix.
plants.harvest: Cut before it becomes a coarse cane. Leave the wet roots alone.
plants.preparation: Hay from high-alkaloid stands is still a poor feed. Do not assume drying makes it safe.
plants.uncertainty: Alkaloid level depends on the variety, which a wild stand does not reveal.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
Penn State Extension, forage and poisonous-plant publications.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It is up early in wet ground, from May, and is coarse by July. Older varieties contain alkaloids. Low-alkaloid varieties exist and look the same.

plants.summary: A perennial garden plant. The leaf blade is an oxalate poison. This guide does not recommend the stalks for animals either.
plants.identification: Huge heart-shaped leaves on thick red or green stalks, dying back in winter.
plants.lookalikes: Swiss chard has a thick midrib but a smaller leaf and is a row crop. Burdock is hairy. If the plant is the rhubarb clump, do not feed the leaf.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves. Do not feed stalks as forage.
plants.harvest: Do not toss the pulled leaves into a pen.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes the leaf safe.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: Stalks are pulled in May and June in New England. The leaves are toxic then and for the rest of the summer.

plants.summary: A low shrub, very common in the region, and seriously poisonous.
plants.identification: A low evergreen shrub, opposite or whorled narrow leaves, and clusters of pink flowers along the stem, not only at the tip.

plants.parts: Do not feed leaves or flowers.
plants.harvest: Do not browse a pasture shrub that looks like this.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes it feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.

plants.summary: A wetland arum. It smells skunky when torn and burns the mouth.
plants.identification: A mottled purple-brown hood in very early spring, then large oval leaves from the mud. Torn leaves smell skunky.
plants.lookalikes: False hellebore is taller, with pleated leaves up a stem, in wet meadows. Both are toxic.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves or roots.
plants.harvest: Do not cut a swamp plant that smells like skunk.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes it feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: The spotted hood appears in early spring, sometimes through snow, in New England swamps. Huge leaves follow in May and June.

plants.summary: A sod-forming hay grass used in New England mixes.
plants.identification: A hairless grass with a drooping, open flower head and a small M-shaped watermark on some young leaves.
plants.lookalikes: Orchardgrass is clumped and the stem base is flattened. Quackgrass has auricles that clasp the stem.
plants.parts: Leaves and stems as hay or fresh cut.
plants.harvest: Cut at early heading. Mature stems are low quality.
plants.preparation: Dry fully for hay, or feed fresh in a mix. Discard mold.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
Penn State Extension, forage and poisonous-plant publications.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: Best leaf is in May and June. It is cut for hay in early summer. Regrowth is modest in a dry August.

plants.summary: A red-fruited sumac. It is not poison sumac. Feeding data are thinner than the identification difference, so the verdict stays limited.
plants.identification: Fuzzy twigs, compound leaves with many leaflets, and upright red fuzzy fruit clusters.
plants.lookalikes: Poison sumac (Toxicodendron vernix) grows in wetlands, has smooth twigs, and bears drooping white berries. If the fruit is white, or the ground is a bog, stop.
plants.parts: Leaves only if you are certain this is staghorn sumac. Not a staple.
plants.harvest: Do not harvest any sumac with white berries. Do not harvest in a swamp.
plants.preparation: There is no preparation that fixes a mix-up with poison sumac.
plants.uncertainty: The toxicology of staghorn sumac as a feed is thin. The poison-sumac distinction is not.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Langston University, E (Kika) de la Garza American Institute for Goat Research, goat nutrition materials.
plants.season_notes: Leaves from June until they redden in September. Red fruit clusters persist into winter. It is a common New England roadside shrub.

verdicts.notes: If the berries are white or the shrubs are standing in a bog, do not cut them.

plants.summary: A mineral-rich green that stings until it is wilted or dried.
plants.identification: Opposite, toothed, heart-shaped leaves and square stems covered in stinging hairs. It grows in damp, rich soil.
plants.lookalikes: Deadnettle and henbit do not sting. Wood nettle has alternate leaves. If you are not sure, do not grab it.
plants.parts: Young tops, after the sting is removed by wilting or drying.
plants.harvest: Cut with gloves. Do not rub the plant into skin.
plants.preparation: Wilt until the leaves are limp, or dry them fully, before they are feed. Fresh unwilted nettle stings mouths.
sources: ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.
Langston University, E (Kika) de la Garza American Institute for Goat Research, goat nutrition materials.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: Cut in May and June before it flowers. By July the stems are fibrous. Wood nettle is a woodland relative and is not this feed.

verdicts.reason: Wilted or dried nettle is a traditional livestock and rabbit green. The sting is mechanical and is gone once the hairs are dried or thoroughly wilted.
verdicts.notes: Do not feed it fresh and crisp. Gloves for the person cutting it.

plants.summary: Not the classic red-maple poisoning tree, and still not a leaf to mix up with red maple.
plants.identification: Opposite leaves with smoother, rounded sinuses and pointed lobes. Buds are brown and sharp. Older bark is plated.
plants.lookalikes: Red maple has sharper teeth, red buds, and often a wetter site. Feed neither if you cannot separate them.
plants.parts: Small winter twigs only, and only when you are sure the tree is sugar maple. Not a pile of leaves.
plants.harvest: Do not feed fallen leaves. Do not feed storm-wilted branches.
plants.preparation: There is no reason to dry the leaves for feed.
plants.uncertainty: Sugar maple leaves have much less published poisoning data than red maple. The limit is there because the two trees are confused and because leaves are an unneeded risk.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: Leaves are on the tree from May to October. Winter twigs are what people actually offer. It is a dominant tree in northern New England woods.

plants.summary: A garden green that is useful and high in oxalate.
plants.identification: Large shiny leaves with a thick white, yellow, or red midrib, on a plant you planted. Beet leaves count.
plants.lookalikes: Rhubarb also has a thick stalk, and the leaf is toxic. Rhubarb leaves are broader and the plant is a large clump that dies to the ground. Do not mix them up.
plants.parts: Leaves, sparingly.
plants.harvest: Cut a few leaves, not a daily diet of chard.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh and limited. Drying does not remove oxalate.
sources: House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: Leaves are cut from July until frost. Beet greens are the same plant species and the same oxalate limit.

plants.summary: A tough pasture grass. The endophyte, not the leaf shape, is the feeding problem.
plants.identification: Coarse dark leaves, prominent veins, and often a reddish base. It grows in clumps.
plants.lookalikes: Orchardgrass has a flattened stem and a branched seed head. Reed canarygrass prefers wetter soil and has a more open seed head.
plants.parts: Leaves, if you use it at all. Do not make a suspect stand the whole diet.
plants.harvest: If you cut it, keep the amount small and mix it with other forage.
plants.preparation: Drying does not remove the endophyte toxin.
plants.uncertainty: Endophyte status of a given plant cannot be judged by eye.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
Penn State Extension, forage and poisonous-plant publications.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It grows from May through October and stays green late. Many older New England pastures are endophyte-infected. The fungus is invisible.

verdicts.label: Rabbit
verdicts.reason: Tall fescue endophyte produces ergovaline. In cattle and sheep it is tied to heat stress, poor gain, and reproductive trouble. You cannot see the infection.
verdicts.notes: A little in a mixed pasture is common. Do not feed a heavy stand as the only forage. Endophyte-free and novel-endophyte varieties exist, but a plant in a field does not show which it is.

plants.summary: A pyrrolizidine-alkaloid ragwort. Liver damage is cumulative.
plants.identification: A biennial with a ragged yellow flower cluster and deeply lobed leaves. The plant is coarse and bitter.
plants.lookalikes: Tansy (Tanacetum) has button flowers and is also not a feed. Goldenrods have different flower heads. Do not feed a yellow late-summer weed on a guess.
plants.parts: Do not feed fresh plants or hay that contains them.
plants.harvest: Pull it out of a cutting.
plants.preparation: Drying does not remove the alkaloids.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
Penn State Extension, forage and poisonous-plant publications.
plants.season_notes: It flowers in mid to late summer in New England pastures and on disturbed ground. The alkaloid remains in hay.

verdicts.notes: Do not use resistance as a reason to cut ragwort for goats.

plants.summary: A standard cool-season hay grass of New England fields.
plants.identification: A dense, cylindrical seed head like a small bottle brush. The stem base has a small swollen corm. The shoot is rolled.
plants.lookalikes: Orchardgrass grows in clumps and has a more open flower head. Reed canarygrass is taller and prefers wetter ground.
plants.parts: Leaves and fine stems, fresh or as hay.
plants.harvest: Cut above the crown and leave stubble. Skip roadsides and any field sprayed with herbicide.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh in a mix, or dry it fully. Do not feed moldy hay.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
University of New Hampshire Extension, pasture and livestock guidance.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: Growth starts in May. The main hay cut in New England is often in June, with a second growth through August. Quality falls once the seed head is mature.

plants.summary: The vine is a nightshade. Leaves and green fruit are not feed.
plants.identification: A hairy, strong-smelling vine you planted, with yellow flowers and green fruit that ripens red, yellow, or another ripe color.
plants.lookalikes: Horsenettle is spiny and wild. Potato vines are a separate toxic entry. Do not feed any of them.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves, stems, or green fruit.
plants.harvest: Do not toss suckers and prunings into a pen.
plants.preparation: Ripe red fruit, seeds and all, is sometimes a small treat for chickens and pigs. It is not forage, and it is not a rabbit food in this guide.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: Vines are up from June until frost. Green fruit and leaves are the problem all season. Ripe fruit is late summer.

plants.summary: A native vine. The berries and leaves are not feed.
plants.identification: Five leaflets from one point, and a vine that climbs with adhesive disks. Berries are dark blue on red stalks.
plants.lookalikes: Poison ivy has three leaflets. If you see three, stop and do not touch it. Five leaflets point here, which is still not a feed.
plants.parts: Do not feed leaves or berries.
plants.harvest: Do not pull it down into a pen as browse.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes it feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center toxic-plant list, used here as a companion-animal caution alongside a veterinary source.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It covers New England fences and woods edges from June until the leaves turn red in September. Berries ripen dark in the fall.

plants.summary: Often called the most poisonous plant in North America. The root is the worst part, and the rest still is not feed.
plants.identification: A hairless, sometimes purple-streaked stem, divided leaves, white flower clusters, and a wet-ground habit. The root, cut lengthwise, shows chambers.
plants.lookalikes: Poison hemlock is the upland spotted plant. Angelica and other white umbels are not safe guesses. Do not dig wet-ground parsleys.
plants.parts: Do not feed roots, stems, or leaves.
plants.harvest: Do not pull it for feed. The root is especially dangerous.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes it feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It grows in New England marshes, ditches, and wet meadows and is dangerous from the time it leafs out in May until it dies back.

plants.summary: A woodland plant with poisonous berries and roots.
plants.identification: Compound leaves, a small cluster of white flowers, then white berries on thick red stalks, each berry with a black dot. Red baneberry has red berries.
plants.lookalikes: False Solomon's seal has a different flower cluster and is not a feed in this guide. Do not feed woodland berries to animals.
plants.parts: Do not feed berries, roots, or leaves.
plants.harvest: Do not gather it.
plants.preparation: No preparation makes it feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It flowers in late spring in rich New England woods. The white berries with black dots, doll's eyes, are obvious later in summer. Red baneberry (Actaea rubra) gets the same verdict.

plants.summary: The common clover of New England lawns and pastures.
plants.identification: Three leaflets, often with a pale crescent, and a white flower head on a leafless stalk. It creeps and roots at the nodes.
plants.lookalikes: Red clover is upright with a pink head. Alsike clover has a pink-and-white head and no crescent mark. Wood sorrel has heart-shaped leaflets and a sour taste.
plants.parts: Leaves and flowers, in limited amounts.
plants.harvest: Pick from places that are not sprayed. Do not harvest a pure stand as the only feed for goats, sheep, or cattle.
plants.preparation: Wilt it a little for ruminants to reduce bloat. Fresh small amounts are the usual rabbit and poultry use. Moldy clover is not feed.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
plants.season_notes: It flowers from June into September. The lush May and June growth is the highest bloat risk for ruminants.

verdicts.label: Rabbit
verdicts.reason: Lush clover causes frothy bloat in cattle, sheep, and goats. Rabbits and guinea pigs bloat or get soft stools from too much clover. A cyanide concern also appears in stressed or wilted clover.
verdicts.notes: A small handful in a mixed bundle is the usual limit. Do not feed a clover-only cutting to ruminants.

plants.summary: One of the better tree leaves for rabbits and goats.
plants.identification: Alternate leaves, variously lobed or heart-shaped, often on the same tree, with milky sap and a berry that looks like a pale blackberry.
plants.lookalikes: Basswood leaves are larger and heart-shaped without the mixed lobes, and the sap is not milky. White snakeroot is a short herb, not a tree.
plants.parts: Leaves. Ripe fruit is a small treat for poultry and pigs.
plants.harvest: Clip leafy twigs. The milky sap is normal for mulberry and is not the milkweed warning.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh or dry the leaves. No wilting step is required.
sources: House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
Langston University, E (Kika) de la Garza American Institute for Goat Research, goat nutrition materials.
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
plants.season_notes: Leaves from late May through September. Fruit in early summer. It is a common invasive tree in southern and coastal New England and is planted elsewhere in the region.

plants.summary: Oaks are common in southern and central New England and in warmer pockets north. Tannins are the problem.
plants.identification: Alternate lobed leaves. White oak has rounded lobes. Red oak has pointed lobes. Acorns sit in a cap.
plants.lookalikes: Maple leaves are opposite. Beech has smooth bark and a simple toothless leaf edge that is not lobed like an oak.
plants.parts: Not young leaves, and not a meal of acorns.
plants.harvest: Do not shake a tree full of green acorns into a pen.
plants.preparation: There is no home step that removes tannins from a pile of acorns.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
Penn State Extension, forage and poisonous-plant publications.
plants.season_notes: Young leaves in May and June and acorns in September and October are the risky parts. Red oaks (pointed lobes) are often worse than white oaks. Both are limited here.

verdicts.label: Rabbit

verdicts.notes: A mouthful of mature leaf is not the same as a diet of acorns. Do not feed acorns as a crop.

plants.summary: A woodland plant that poisons animals and can poison people who drink the milk of animals that ate it.
plants.identification: Opposite leaves with three main veins and toothed edges, and flat clusters of white flower heads. It grows in shade.
plants.lookalikes: Boneset has leaves that the stem appears to grow through. Late white woodland flowers should not be fed on a guess.
plants.parts: Do not feed any part.
plants.harvest: Do not add it to browse from a woods edge.
plants.preparation: Drying does not make it safe. Do not use the milk of an animal that may have eaten it.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It flowers in late summer and fall in New England woods and edges. The toxin passes into milk, which is the historical milk-sickness story.

plants.summary: A tall yellow umbel. The plant is phototoxic to stock and to the person cutting it.
plants.identification: A grooved stem, pinnate leaves, and flat yellow flower clusters. It is a biennial, with a rosette the first year.
plants.lookalikes: Golden alexanders bloom earlier and are smaller. Queen Anne's lace has white flowers. Poison hemlock has white flowers and purple-spotted stems.
plants.parts: Do not feed any part. Do not get sap on skin.
plants.harvest: If you must handle it, cover skin and wash off sap. Do not put it in the feed basket.
plants.preparation: There is no safe preparation for feed.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
plants.season_notes: It flowers on New England roadsides in July and August. Sap on skin plus sunlight causes severe burns in people. That is a harvest hazard, not only a feeding one.

plants.summary: A standard browse for rabbits and goats. Salicylates are the reason not to feed a diet of bark.
plants.identification: Alternate, narrow leaves on flexible twigs, often along water. Buds are covered by a single scale.
plants.lookalikes: Brittle willow lookalikes are still willows. Cherry twigs have a bitter-almond smell when scratched and are a different, toxic entry.
plants.parts: Twigs and leaves, in moderation. Not a pile of bark.
plants.harvest: Cut finger-thick twigs. Do not girdle a tree you want to keep.
plants.preparation: Feed fresh. Dried leafy twigs are fine. Do not feed a large amount of bark.
sources: House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
Langston University, E (Kika) de la Garza American Institute for Goat Research, goat nutrition materials.
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
plants.season_notes: Twigs are cut from late winter through summer. Pussy willow (Salix discolor) and black willow (Salix nigra) are common New England species. Leaves are best before midsummer.

plants.summary: A tall roadside legume. Moldy sweet-clover hay causes a clotting failure.
plants.identification: Tall, branched, with small yellow flowers in narrow clusters and a sweet smell when crushed. Leaves are in threes.
plants.lookalikes: White sweet clover is the same problem with white flowers. Alfalfa has purple flowers and does not smell the same.
plants.parts: Not a preferred fresh feed. Spoiled hay is dangerous.
plants.harvest: Do not bale it wet. Do not feed stems that heated or molded.
plants.preparation: Fresh plants are a limited green. Any moldy sweet-clover hay should be thrown out, not diluted.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
plants.season_notes: Tall plants flower along New England roadsides in July and August. The bleeding problem is in spoiled hay, not in a fresh handful.

verdicts.label: Rabbit
verdicts.reason: Moldy sweet clover makes dicoumarol, which stops blood from clotting. Cattle are the classic victims. Fresh, unspoiled plants do not have that toxin, but they are not a chosen staple.
verdicts.notes: If the cutting smells moldy or heated, do not feed it to any animal.

plants.summary: Yew is extremely poisonous. A handful of clippings can kill.
plants.identification: Flat, dark needles, a red fleshy cup around a single seed, and a shrub habit. Cultivated yews are often sheared foundation plants.
plants.lookalikes: Eastern hemlock (Tsuga canadensis) is a tree with short flat needles and small cones. It is not yew and it is not poison hemlock, and it is not a feed in this guide. If you are looking at foundation-shrub clippings, assume yew until you know otherwise.
plants.parts: Do not feed needles, twigs, or seeds.
plants.harvest: Do not dump hedge trimmings into a pasture or a rabbit run.
plants.preparation: There is no safe amount and no drying step.
sources: Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock.
Merck Veterinary Manual, toxicology and species nutrition chapters.
ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center toxic-plant list, used here as a companion-animal caution alongside a veterinary source.
plants.season_notes: Canada yew is a native understory shrub, green whenever it is not buried in snow. The yews that kill animals in New England are often Japanese or English yew planted around houses. All of them count as this entry, all year.

verdicts.label: Rabbit
verdicts.reason: Taxine alkaloids. Yew causes sudden death in livestock. Canada yew and the cultivated yews are all dangerous. The red cup does not make the seed or the needles safe.
verdicts.notes: Do not feed any part. Do not compost clippings where animals can reach them.
